area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: A model name is resolved to a provider by walking a fixed 7-entry priority list (GOOGLE, OPENAI, AZURE, XAI, DIAL, CUSTOM, OPENROUTER) and returning the first registered+instantiable provider whose validate_model_name() returns True; there is no name→provider index.

area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: conf/xai_models.json declares max_output_tokens equal to context_window for both entries (grok-4: 256000/256000; grok-4-1-fast-reasoning: 2000000/2000000), a shape no other manifest uses and one that no vendor offers.
evidence: json dump of conf/xai_models.json: grok-4 context_window=256000 max_output_tokens=256000; grok-4-1-fast-reasoning context_window=2000000 max_output_tokens=2000000
by contrast conf/gemini_models.json: context_window 1048576 with max_output_tokens 65536; conf/openai_models.json gpt-5: 400000 / 128000
providers/shared/model_capabilities.py:96-99 (max_output_tokens ≥ 65_000 adds +2 to the capability rank)
why: Token budgeting and auto-mode ranking both read max_output_tokens, so an inflated figure both mis-sizes the response reserve and pushes the model up the ranking — and this is the concrete example of what 'stale against the real vendor' costs.

refutation.reason: The raw numbers check out (grok-4 256000/256000, grok-4-1-fast-reasoning 2000000/2000000), but every load-bearing premise around them fails. (1) "A shape no other manifest uses" is false: conf/openrouter_models.json contains four entries where max_output_tokens == context_window, and two of them are not xAI at all — meta-llama/llama-3-70b (8192/8192) and perplexity/llama-3-sonar-large-32k-online (32768/32768) — which predate the grok entries entirely. (2) The framing "the PAL MCP fork declares" implies fork provenance; git log --all on conf/xai_models.json shows only four commits, all authored upstream by Fahad <fahad@2doapp.com> for BeehiveInnovations (514c9c5 "feat: grok-4.1 support ... issues/339", 8b16405, b2dc849, 2a706d5). The fork has never touched the file on any branch. (3) The cited consequence does not bite. providers/shared/model_capabilities.py:96-99 saturates the output bonus at +2 for anything >= 65_000, so grok-4 and grok-4.1 receive exactly the same +2 as gemini-2.5-pro (65536) and gpt-5 (128000) — the very entries the claim contrasts them with. The "inflated" numbers buy zero rank advantage. Recomputing get_effective_capability_rank with a conservative 64000 moves grok-4 from 90 to 89 and grok-4.1 from 86 to 85, changing no ordering. (4) The value never reaches the wire: every generate_content call site (tools/simple/base.py:444, tools/workflow/workflow_mixin.py:1493, tools/consensus.py:618) omits max_output_tokens, so providers/openai_compatible.py:436-437
refutation.corrected_statement: conf/xai_models.json sets max_output_tokens equal to context_window for both grok entries (256000 and 2000000), which is almost certainly wrong as a vendor fact about output limits. But it is inherited verbatim from upstream BeehiveInnovations (commit 514c9c5 and earlier), not fork-introduced; the same equal-values shape already appears in conf/openrouter_models.json for four models including two non-xAI ones; and it is inert at runtime — the value is never passed to generate_content and therefore never sent as max_tokens/max_completion_tokens, while its sole consumer, the >= 65_000 output bonus at providers/shared/model_capabilities.py:96-99, saturates at +2 and so grants grok no ranking advantage over gemini-2.5-pro (65536) or gpt-5 (128000). Correcting the values would change the capability rank by 1 point out of 100 and reorder nothing.

area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: parser and runner are not fields of CLIClientConfig at all — they come only from clink/constants.py INTERNAL_DEFAULTS, keyed by the lowercased 'name'. A config whose name is not one of the seven internal keys is a hard RegistryLoadError("CLI 'x' is not supported by clink"), so a new CLI cannot be added by dropping in a JSON file. The registry's own 'must define a parser either in configuration or internal defaults' error is unreachable, since CLIInternalDefaults.parser has no default and every entry sets it.

clink/constants.py:29-92 (all seven entries: gemini, codex, claude, claude-9arm, antigravity, cursor, opencode — each sets parser)

area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: Configs are loaded from three search paths in order — the bundled conf/cli_clients dir, then CLI_CLIENTS_CONFIG_PATH (file or directory), then ~/.pal/cli_clients — and a later file with the same lowercased 'name' silently replaces the earlier one (logged only at INFO). This machine has a live override: ~/.pal/cli_clients/cursor.json replaces the bundled cursor command with an absolute cursor-agent.cmd path and injects env {"SHELL": "C:/WINDOWS/system32/cmd.exe"}.

area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: Cost accounting is declared per-CLI-client: RateCard carries a mandatory `unit` string (e.g. 'USD' or 'credits') and `per_tokens` (default 1_000_000), and prices four token classes — input, cached_input, output, reasoning_output — each individually optional. price_call returns either CallCost(value, unit, unpriced_classes) or CostUnavailable with one of four machine-readable reasons: no_rate_card, model_unresolved, no_usage_reported, model_not_priced.

area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: No file in the repository declares a rate_card. The only occurrences of the string are in code (clink/models.py, pricing.py, registry.py, agents/base.py, tools/clink.py), tests (3 files), docs (CHANGES-FORK.md, DONE.md, an Obsidian note) and logs — so price_call returns CostUnavailable(no_rate_card) for every client, and tools/clink.py deliberately suppresses that one reason, meaning the caller is given no cost field and no explanation.

area: Model providers and configuration (providers/, conf/, config.py, environment-variable hand
statement: Every clink subprocess receives a full copy of PAL's own environment: _build_environment() is os.environ.copy() updated with the client's declared env, with no allowlist, denylist or redaction — so GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, DIAL_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY and CUSTOM_API_KEY are all handed to the foreign agent binary (codex, cursor, agy, claude, opencode).

clink/agents/antigravity.py:123,129,190 (same _build_environment, passed to winpty.PtyProcess.spawn)

The caps are: MAX_RESPONSE_CHARS = 20_000 (tools/clink.py:46), the threshold at which `_apply_output_limit` fires on the success path and also the per-field bound `_store_diagnostic` applies to salvaged_content/stdout/stderr on the non-zero-exit path; an excerpt bound of min(4000, MAX_RESPONSE_CHARS // 2) = 4000 chars (tools/clink.py:662), which is what a truncated response actually carries when the CLI emitted no <SUMMARY>; and MAX_DRAINED_OUTPUT_CHARS = 10_000 (clink/agents/base.py:71), which bounds the stdout/stderr tail of a timed-out run because the error path never reaches `_apply_output_limit`. Confirmed unrelated to output: MCP_PROMPT_SIZE_LIMIT (config.py:142, derived from MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS) is applied only to user input.

statement: clink's summarisation is not compression: when output exceeds the cap and a <SUMMARY> block exists, the returned content becomes the summary text alone — every word outside the tags, including the analysis that produced it, is discarded and only its character count is reported.
evidence: tools/clink.py:626-651 — `summary = self._extract_summary(content)`; on hit it returns `summary_text` with metadata output_summarized/output_original_length/output_summary_length
tools/clink.py:683-688 — _extract_summary returns only `SUMMARY_PATTERN.search(content).group(1)`

systemprompts/clink/default.txt:8 — the role prompt is what makes the block exist: "Always conclude with `<SUMMARY>...</SUMMARY>` containing a terse (≤500 words) recap"
tools/clink.py:653-681 — with no <SUMMARY>, the fallback is an explanatory message plus a head excerpt of `min(4000, 10000)` chars
why: The quality of a large delegation collapses to whatever the foreign CLI chose to put in ≤500 words; a PAL feature that wants the reasoning (not the verdict) must either raise the cap or stream, and neither exists today.

refutation.reason: Every cited line checks out and I could not find any path that contradicts it. tools/clink.py:617-651: once len(content) > MAX_RESPONSE_CHARS (20_000, a module constant with no env/config override) and SUMMARY_PATTERN hits, `_apply_output_limit` returns `summary_text` alone — the group(1) capture, stripped — with metadata output_summarized / output_original_length / output_summary_length / output_limit. I executed the function against the repo venv with a 25,049-char body containing `<SUMMARY>the recap</SUMMARY>` plus trailing text: it returned exactly `'the recap'` (9 chars); the body was absent from the return value AND from every metadata value (`_prune_metadata(..., reason="summary")` drops events/raw/raw_events rather than capping them). I searched wider than the original: only one clink implementation exists (`find . -name "clink*.py"` → ./tools/clink.py), there is no second summarisation code path in clink/, tools/, utils/, providers/ or server.py, no worktrees, and the agent's temp output file is read then unlink()ed (clink/agents/base.py:305-311), so the discarded text does not survive on disk. The repo's own test asserts the behaviour (tests/test_clink_tool.py:110-149: content == "This is the condensed summary." for a cap+500-char input). Two additional facts make the claim stronger than stated: the post-limit `content` is what gets written into the conversation thread (`_record_turn_and_total(continuation_id, content, ...)`, tools/clink.py:367), so the body is unre
refutation.corrected_statement: clink does not compress the output itself — it selects and discards. When a CLI response exceeds MAX_RESPONSE_CHARS (20_000, hardcoded at tools/clink.py:46) and contains a `<SUMMARY>` block, `_apply_output_limit` returns the text inside the first matching pair of tags and nothing else (tools/clink.py:626-651): the analysis that produced the summary, and any text after `</SUMMARY>`, are dropped from the response, from the metadata (`raw`/`raw_events`/`events` are removed, not capped), and from the conversation thread — `_record_turn_and_total(continuation_id, content, ...)` at line 367 stores the already-reduced content, so a continuation call cannot recover it either. All that remains of the discarded material is `output_original_length`. The compression is real but happens upstream, in the CLI agent obeying its role prompt ("Always conclude with `<SUMMARY>...</SUMMARY>` … ≤500 words"), which 3 of the 4 shipped clink role prompts carry — `default_planner.txt` does not, so planner runs fall through to the truncation path (an explanatory message plus a 4000-char head excerpt, `min(4000, MAX_RESPONSE_CHARS // 2)`). Because the extraction uses `search`, the first `<SUMMARY>` in the stream wins, so a quoted or mid-output block can be returned in place of the final recap.

refutation.corrected_statement:
The claim holds as stated; only its citations and its description of the consequence need sharpening.

Precise version: The simulator harness cannot find this repo's virtualenv on Windows. Two byte-identical `_get_python_path()` implementations — simulator_tests/base_test.py:32-53 and communication_simulator_test.py:134-155 (the claim cited 35-52 and 133-153, each shifted by one to two lines) — probe only `os.path.join(cwd, X, "bin", "python")` for X in {`.venv`, `venv`, `.pal_venv`} and never `Scripts/python.exe`, so on Windows they always log "Virtual environment not found, using system python" and return the bare string `"python"`. Confirmed by execution: with `.venv/Scripts/python.exe` present and `.venv/bin/python` absent, the resolved path is `'python'`. Because `os.path.exists` performs no PATHEXT resolution, not even a hypothetical `.venv\bin\python.exe` could match.

Two corrections/additions to the claim's framing:

1. The consequence is not uniform across the two copies. In communication_simulator_test.py the bare fallback is not silently used — `_verify_server_environment` at line 234 tests `os.path.exists(self.python_path)`, which is False for `"python"`, so it logs "Python executable not found: python" / "Please run ./run-server.sh first to set up the environment" and returns False, aborting the run. In simulator_tests/base_test.py:162 the bare string is passed straight to `subprocess.run` as `[self.python_path, "server.py"]` with no existence check, so it silently launches whatever `python` resolves to on PATH — a different and quieter failure. So: one copy hard-fails with a misleading message, the other silently runs the wrong interpreter.

2. This is an inconsistency within the repo, not a deliberate POSIX-only scope. run-server.sh:91-106 `get_venv_python_path()` already probes both `bin/python` and `Scripts/python.exe`, and run-server.sh:109-122 `detect_os()` explicitly recognises `msys*|cygwin*|win32` as "windows". The bash layer handles the Windows layout; only the Python harness does not. The defect is invisible in CI, which is ubuntu-latest only (.github/workflows/test.yml:9,39).

area: clink subsystem — D:/Github/pal-mcp-server/clink/ (agents, parsers, registry, constants, m
statement: There is no lifecycle hook around the child process: the only seams are refuse_unservable (pre-spawn, argv-only), _build_command/_model_args (argv), _build_environment (env), _recover_from_error (post-exit, non-zero only) and finalize_output (post-parse). Anything needing to observe the child while it runs — streaming, progress, cancellation, per-call cwd — must override run() wholesale, which is what AntigravityAgent does and why it must re-call refuse_unservable by hand.
evidence: clink/agents/base.py: the complete method list of BaseCLIAgent is __init__ 201, run 206, finalize_output 357, refuse_unservable 438, _extract_token_usage 467, _resolve_model_effort 483, _build_command 506, _model_args 523, _build_environment 533, _recover_from_error 542 (whole 558-line file read)
clink/agents/base.py:449-453 the comment explaining refuse_unservable cannot live in _build_command because AntigravityAgent overrides that too
clink/agents/antigravity.py:109-112 'This runner overrides run wholesale, so it inherits nothing from the base loop — the refusal has to be called here too'
why: A streaming or cancellable clink is not an override away; it is a rewrite of run() duplicated per runner, and each duplicate must re-implement the pre-spawn refusal and the finalize contract by hand.

statement: What each parser keeps vs discards: codex_jsonl keeps the concatenated agent_message texts and stores every decoded event under `events` plus `usage` (turn.completed) and `errors`; claude_json keeps `result` (or a message/error fallback) and stores `raw`, `raw_events`, `usage`, `model_usage`, `model_used`, `session_id`, `uuid`, `permission_denials`, durations; gemini_json keeps `response` and stores `raw`, `stats`, `model_used`, `token_usage`, `latency_ms`; opencode_jsonl keeps the `type:"text"` part.text values and ACCUMULATES `part.tokens`/`part.cost` across every step_finish; antigravity_text keeps ANSI-stripped stdout and stores nothing but stderr. Only claude_json and gemini_json ever set `model_used`, i.e. only those two can produce observed_model or a model_substituted flag.

refutation.corrected_statement: This clone has no remote named `upstream` and no `refs/remotes/upstream/*` namespace. `origin` is the fork itself (https://github.com/xenodeve/pal-mcp-server) and is the only remote defined in any config scope — local, global, or system — with no `url.*.insteadOf` rewrite, no `includeIf`/`include.path`, no `extensions.worktreeConfig`, no `objects/info/alternates`, no submodules, and no `GIT_*` env override that could introduce another. The linked worktree at `D:/Github/_pal-readme` shares the common gitdir and defines no remotes of its own. `.git/packed-refs`, `.git/info/refs` (a 13KB stale-ref snapshot), all reflogs, and all 14 lines of `.git/FETCH_HEAD` contain zero upstream references. Two corrections to the original framing: upstream-TRACKING refs do exist in the git sense — 39 branches carry `branch.<n>.remote`/`branch.<n>.merge` and `main@{upstream}` resolves to `origin/main` — so the absent thing is specifically a second remote for the fork parent, not `@{upstream}` configuration. And upstream HISTORY is fully present locally: 76 tags spanning v5.10.0–v9.8.2 of the upstream release train, `v5.11.0` an ancestor of `main`, with upstream-authored commits (Beehive Innovations, Fahad, Sven Lito, Josh Vera) reachable. area: conversation memory and cross-tool threading (PAL MCP fork, D:/Github/pal-mcp-server)
statement: Thread lifetime is a SLIDING TTL of `CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_HOURS * 3600` (code default 3h). Every `add_turn` rewrites the whole thread with a fresh TTL; `get_thread` does NOT refresh it. So an actively-written thread never expires, and a read-only thread dies 3h after its last write.
evidence: utils/conversation_memory.py:135-148 `CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_HOURS` env parse, default "3"; `CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = HOURS * 3600`
utils/conversation_memory.py:384 `storage.setex(key, CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, context.model_dump_json())  # Refresh TTL`
utils/conversation_memory.py:295-305 `get_thread` only calls `storage.get(key)`; no re-set
utils/storage_backend.py:59-71 `get()` deletes on expiry, never extends
why: clink's `_thread_totals` is a pure read. A caller polling costs on an idle thread will watch it vanish at 3h with no warning; only writing a turn keeps a thread alive.

refutation.reason: The TTL mechanism is described correctly, but the load-bearing consequence — "an actively-written thread never expires" — is false, and there is a reachable in-code path that proves it. `add_turn` gates on the turn ceiling BEFORE the `setex` that refreshes the TTL (utils/conversation_memory.py:360-362: `if len(context.turns) >= MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS: ... return False`), so once a thread reaches MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS (code default 50 at :122; the shipped .env.example:163 sets 40) every further write returns False without ever reaching line 384. The thread keeps being served — server.py:1088-1092 only logs a warning on `add_turn` failure and continues to rebuild history and call the model — so it is actively used while its TTL is frozen, and it dies CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS after the last ACCEPTED turn. I verified this empirically against the real module (MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS=2): the first two `add_turn` calls returned True and moved the stored expiry; the third and fourth returned False and the expiry did not move; `get_thread` never moved it. Two secondary inaccuracies: (a) storage is a process-local singleton (utils/storage_backend.py:98-112, "PROCESS-SPECIFIC STORAGE"), so a server restart destroys every thread regardless of TTL — "never expires" is bounded by process lifetime, not only by writes; (b) "default 3h" is the code fallback only — the repo's own .env.example:157 ships CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_HOURS=24, so the operative default for anyone following the setup d
refutation.corrected_statement: Thread lifetime is a sliding TTL of `CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_HOURS * 3600` (code fallback 3h at utils/conversation_memory.py:135-148; the shipped .env.example:157 sets 24h). The TTL slides only on a SUCCESSFUL write: `create_thread` (:265) and `add_turn` (:384) both call `storage.setex(key, CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, context.model_dump_json())`, and `set_with_ttl` recomputes `expires_at = time.time() + ttl_seconds` from scratch (utils/storage_backend.py:52-56). `get_thread` only calls `storage.get` (:298) and never re-sets, and `get()` deletes on expiry without extending (storage_backend.py:59-71) — so reads never refresh. BUT `add_turn` returns False before reaching the setex when the thread is at the turn ceiling (:360-362, MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS, code default 50 / .env.example 40), and server.py:1088-1092 merely logs a warning and serves the request anyway. Therefore a thread that has reached the turn limit remains fully usable while its TTL is frozen, and expires CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS after its last ACCEPTED turn despite continued activity. Correct formulation: a thread expires TIMEOUT after its last accepted WRITE — reads and rejected writes do not extend it — and, because storage is a process-local in-memory singleton (storage_backend.py:98-112), all threads are additionally destroyed on server restart regardless of remaining TTL.

statement: Every read and every write deserialises/serialises the WHOLE thread. A single `chat` continuation performs roughly nine full `ThreadContext.model_validate_json` parses and two full `model_dump_json` writes of the entire conversation; a `clink` continuation performs about five and two. Cost is O(turns) per operation, O(turns^2) per conversation.

refutation.reason: Survived every break attempt, and I verified it two independent ways: by reading the full call chain, and by executing the chain. (1) Import-time execution: `reload_env()` is a bare module-scope call at utils/env.py:57, and utils.env is imported by server.py:72, config.py:11, clink/registry.py:27 and every providers/*.py, so it runs in the server process and specifically on the clink path. (3) The `override=False` default is not a mitigation: the installed dotenv's `set_as_environment_variables` reads `if k in os.environ and not self.override: continue` / `if v is not None: os.environ[k] = v` — keys absent from the parent are written unconditionally; `override` only decides whose value wins, not whether the key lands. (4) I searched specifically for a mitigation between load and spawn and found none: `_build_environment()` (clink/agents/base.py:533-536) is `os.environ.copy()` + `env.update(self.client.env)` with no allowlist, denylist, or redaction; it is defined exactly once with NO subclass overrides; and both production spawn paths reach it — clink/agents/base.py:271 (`asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(..., env=env)`) and clink/agents/antigravity.py:190 (`winpty.PtyProcess.spawn(..., env=env)`, which overrides `run` wholesale but still calls `
refutation.corrected_statement: PAL's `.env` is read into `os.environ` at import time and every key it sets is then handed to foreign CLI subprocesses. `utils/env.py:57` calls `reload_env()` at module scope; `utils.env` is imported by `server.py:72`, `config.py:11` and `clink/registry.py:27`, so this runs in the server process and on the clink path. `reload_env()` calls `load_dotenv(dotenv_path=_ENV_PATH, override=_FORCE_ENV_OVERRIDE)` whenever the fixed, non-redirectable `_PROJECT_ROOT/.env` (utils/env.py:16-17) exists. `override=False` is not a mitigation: dotenv writes any key not already present in `os.environ`, and `override` only decides whose value wins. `clink/agents/base.py:533-536` then does `os.environ.copy()` + `env.update(self.client.env)` with no allowlist, denylist, or redaction; it has no subclass overrides, `client.env` is `{}` in all eight shipped configs, and both — and only — production spawn paths pass that env explicitly (`base.py:271` asyncio, `antigravity.py:190` winpty). Precision: a `None`-valued bare `KEY` line is skipped, and a key already in `os.environ` keeps the parent's value (the key still reaches the child; only the value differs), so the exact statement is "every key that dotenv sets" rather than "every key in the file". The claim also understates the risk in one direction: `PAL_MCP_FORCE_ENV_OVERRIDE=true` makes `.env` values overwrite the parent's, and no configuration flag anywhere disables the `os.environ` write. As the original boundary states, this clone has no `.env` today, so the mechanism is verified from code and from execution while current key flow on this machine is not; on a deployment following the documented setup path (SECURITY.md:72) the flow is unconditional and cross-vendor — e.g. `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `XAI_API_KEY` are handed to Codex, and `OPENAI_API_KEY` to the Gemini CLI.

area: Security posture of the PAL MCP fork, with emphasis on the clink subprocess boundary (envi
statement: On Windows, a caller-supplied `model` string can break out of its argument and execute arbitrary commands, because the resolved executables are `.cmd` batch shims and Python's `list2cmdline` escaping (`\"`) is not honoured by cmd.exe.
evidence: Resolved executable observed as a batch shim in this repo's own log: `grep -ohE "Executing CLI command: [^ ]+" logs/mcp_server.log | sort -u` → `C:/Users/xenod/AppData/Local/cursor-agent/cursor-agent.cmd`

clink/discovery.py:22-30 `_KNOWN_LOCATIONS` points three more clients at shims: claude → `%APPDATA%
pm\claude.cmd`, codex → `%APPDATA%
pm\codex.cmd`, gemini → `%APPDATA%
pm\gemini.cmd`
Escaping verified: `.venv/Scripts/python.exe -c "import subprocess; print(subprocess.list2cmdline([...,'--model','gpt-5\" & whoami & \"']))"` → `... --model "gpt-5\" & whoami & \""`

cmd.exe parse verified by running: `cmd /c 'echo "a\" & echo INJECTED_PROOF & echo \""'` → three lines, the middle one `INJECTED_PROOF` — cmd.exe treated `&` as a separator because `\"` closed the quote

CPython 3.11.9 (`sys.version` from .venv) does no batch-file escaping for shell=False: `grep -n -i "\.bat|\.cmd|comspec|batch" <stdlib>/subprocess.py` → only lines 1518-1529, which are inside the `shell=True` branch
why: If it holds, a hostile or prompt-injected `model` argument is host command execution that does not even require the (already bypassed) CLI's own tool permissions — it runs before the agent starts. The mitigation is cheap and independent of the trust epic: validate `model`/`reasoning_effort` against a character class, or make `model_catalog` mandatory (ARG-2), or resolve past the shim to the real `.exe`.
search_boundary: Every component is verified individually (shim resolution from the live log; list2cmdline output; cmd.exe's treatment of `\"` + `&`; absence of stdlib batch escaping). The end-to-end exploit was NOT executed — I did not issue a clink call with a hostile `model`, and I did not confirm that CreateProcess routes these specific `.cmd` files through cmd.exe on this box. Treat as a strong hypothesis requiring one controlled test, not as a demonstrated exploit.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: PAL advertises exactly two capabilities — tools and prompts — via a hand-written `ServerCapabilities(...)` literal, bypassing the SDK's `Server.get_capabilities()`. `listChanged` is left unset on both, and `resources`, `logging`, `completions`, and `experimental` are never populated.
evidence: server.py:1504-1511 `InitializationOptions(server_name="PAL", server_version=__version__, instructions=handshake_instructions, capabilities=ServerCapabilities(tools=ToolsCapability(), prompts=PromptsCapability()))`
`.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/types.py:455-460` `class ToolsCapability: listChanged: bool | None = None` → the no-arg constructor advertises nothing
`.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/server/lowlevel/server.py:193-237` `get_capabilities()` derives capabilities from registered handlers — PAL never calls it
why: Two consequences someone will hit: (1) registering a resources/logging/completions handler later will NOT be advertised unless this literal is also edited — a silent no-op class of bug; (2) with `listChanged` unset PAL can never legally tell a host its tool list changed, so the model list baked into each tool's `model` description is frozen at the host's first `tools/list` for the life of the connection.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: `list_tools` builds each `Tool` from four fields only — `name`, `description`, `inputSchema`, `annotations` — where name/description come from `get_name()`/`get_description()` cached on the instance at construction. `Tool.title`, `Tool.outputSchema` and `_meta` are never set.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: Schemas are hand-built JSON Schema dicts. All 18 tools override `get_input_schema()`; two shared builders (`tools/shared/schema_builders.py:SchemaBuilder.build_schema` for simple tools, `tools/workflow/schema_builders.py:WorkflowSchemaBuilder.build_schema` for workflow tools) supply common fields, and each tool passes a `tool_specific_fields` dict of literal JSON Schema fragments on top. Nothing is generated from Pydantic.
evidence: `grep -rn 'def get_input_schema' tools/*.py` → 18 files, one per registered tool
tools/shared/schema_builders.py:54-105 build_schema; tools/workflow/schema_builders.py:82-155 build_schema
tools/analyze.py:174-200 — override that calls `WorkflowSchemaBuilder` with `analyze_field_overrides` written as literal dicts

Parallel Pydantic model for the same tool: tools/analyze.py:82-118 `class AnalyzeWorkflowRequest(WorkflowRequest)` with `analysis_type: Optional[Literal['architecture','performance','security','quality','general']]` — the same five values also hand-written at tools/analyze.py:232 as `"enum": [...]`
`pydantic>=2.0.0` is already a hard dependency (pyproject.toml:14)
why: Every tool maintains its wire schema and its validation model twice, by hand, with no test tying them together. `model_json_schema()` on the request model would collapse the two; today only convention keeps `Literal[...]` and `"enum": [...]` in agreement, and a drift is invisible until a host rejects a valid call (or accepts an invalid one).

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: The `model` parameter is typed `{"type": "string"}` with no `enum`, even though the function that builds it has already computed the concrete list of available models — it renders them into the *description* prose instead.
evidence: tools/shared/base_tool.py:526-570 `get_model_field_schema()`: calls `summaries, total, restricted = self._get_ranked_model_summaries()`, formats `f"{label}: {top_line}; +{remainder} more via `listmodels`."` into `description`, and returns `{"type": "string", "description": description}` in both the auto-mode and fixed-model branches
By contrast, every other constrained field does use enum: tools/shared/schema_builders.py:32 thinking_mode, tools/clink.py:206 `"enum": self._cli_names`, tools/clink.py:211 roles
why: A wrong model name is caught only at execution, after the host has committed the call; with an `enum` the SDK's own `jsonschema.validate` (CALL-01) would reject it at the boundary for free, and hosts could offer completion. The truncation ("+N more via listmodels") exists precisely because prose has no room — an enum has no such limit. This is also the one place MCP's `completions` capability would pay for itself.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: Schema strictness is inconsistent across tools, and it is load-bearing because the SDK validates input against `inputSchema`. Most tools emit `additionalProperties: False` plus a `$schema` draft-07 declaration; `challenge` emits neither; `clink` emits `additionalProperties: False` but no `$schema`; only workflow tools get a `title`.
evidence: tools/shared/schema_builders.py:95-99 and tools/workflow/schema_builders.py:144-149 both set `"$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"` and `"additionalProperties": False`
tools/workflow/schema_builders.py:152-153 `if tool_name: schema["title"] = f"{tool_name.capitalize()}Request"` — simple tools never pass tool_name
tools/challenge.py:96-105 returns `{"type": "object", "properties": {...}, "required": ["prompt"]}` — no additionalProperties, no $schema
tools/clink.py:236-245 sets `additionalProperties: False` and `required`, no `$schema`
why: Because `@server.call_tool()` defaults to `validate_input=True` (CALL-01), `challenge` silently accepts junk arguments that every other tool rejects. The difference is not cosmetic — it is a per-tool difference in what the host is allowed to send, produced by nobody's decision.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: `clink`'s schema advertises an `images` parameter and its execute path then refuses every call that uses it.
evidence: tools/clink.py:216 `"images": SchemaBuilder.COMMON_FIELD_SCHEMAS["images"]` in the advertised properties
tools/clink.py:292-299 `if images: self._raise_tool_error("clink does not support the `images` parameter: the underlying CLIs take a text prompt only, so images are silently dropped rather than …")`
CHANGES-FORK.md / README.md:11 record this as a fork fix — the previous behaviour was a silent drop
why: The fork correctly turned a silent drop into a loud error, but stopped one step short: the parameter is still in the published schema, so a host will keep offering it and keep paying a round trip to be told no. Removing the key from the properties dict makes the refusal unreachable and the contract honest.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: All 18 tools carry annotations, and `readOnlyHint` is the only annotation field any of them ever sets. Defaults come from the class hierarchy: `SimpleTool` (tools/simple/base.py:104-117) and `WorkflowTool` (tools/workflow/base.py:113-126) both return `{"readOnlyHint": True}`; `BaseTool` returns `None` (tools/shared/base_tool.py:205-217) but both direct BaseTool subclasses override it. `chat` is the only tool whose hint is False.
evidence: Overrides: tools/chat.py:81-84 `return {"readOnlyHint": False}`; tools/clink.py:156-157 `return {"readOnlyHint": True}`; tools/listmodels.py:50-52 and tools/version.py:154-156 `return {"readOnlyHint": True}`

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: `clink` declares `readOnlyHint: True` while its shipped client configs launch foreign agents with approvals and sandboxing bypassed. No test anywhere asserts any annotation value.
evidence: tools/clink.py:156-157 `def get_annotations(self) -> dict[str, Any]: return {"readOnlyHint": True}`
conf/cli_clients/codex.json:3-8 `"additional_args": ["--json", "--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox", "--enable", "web_search_request"]`
conf/cli_clients/gemini.json:3-6 `"additional_args": ["--yolo"]`
SDK contract for the field: `.venv/.../mcp/types.py:1262-1266` "If true, the tool does not modify its environment."
`grep -rn readOnlyHint tests/ simulator_tests/` → no output (zero occurrences)

Already recorded as untracked work: docs/OPEN-WORK-LEDGER.md:198-200 "🔴 `readOnlyHint` is inaccurate … Fix the annotation to match agentic behavior" — sourced from the 2026-07-16 architecture review, still not a GitHub issue

Hosts use readOnlyHint for auto-approval policy; PAL is telling every host that its single most dangerous tool — spawn a foreign agent with the sandbox off, in the live working directory — modifies nothing. It has been known since 2026-07-16 and is neither ticketed nor tested. Correct shape: `readOnlyHint: False`, `destructiveHint: True`, `openWorldHint: True`.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: PAL registers `@server.call_tool()` with no arguments, which in the pinned SDK means `validate_input=True`: the SDK looks the tool up in the cache populated by `list_tools` and runs `jsonschema.validate(arguments, tool.inputSchema)` before PAL's handler is entered. PAL performs no schema validation of its own — its second line of defence is the Pydantic request model inside `tool.execute`.
evidence: server.py:692 `@server.call_tool()`

`.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/server/lowlevel/server.py:498-545`: `def call_tool(self, *, validate_input: bool = True)`; handler does `tool = await self._get_cached_tool_definition(tool_name)`, then `if validate_input and tool: jsonschema.validate(instance=arguments, schema=tool.inputSchema)` → on failure returns `_make_error_result(f"Input validation error: {e.message}")`
PAL-side: server.py:749-880 does routing, model resolution and file-size checks — no jsonschema call anywhere in the repo (`grep -rn jsonschema --include=*.py .` outside .venv: none)
why: Every quality of the hand-written schemas is enforced behavior, not documentation — including the inconsistencies in SCHEMA-03. It also means a schema/Pydantic drift (SCHEMA-01) produces a rejection at the SDK boundary that PAL's own error path never sees and never logs.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: Tool errors reach the host as `CallToolResult(isError=True)` whose single TextContent is the JSON body of PAL's `ToolOutput` envelope. The mechanism is: PAL raises `ToolExecutionError(payload_json)`; the SDK's call_tool wrapper catches every exception and returns `_make_error_result(str(e))`. There is no JSON-RPC error and no error code for tool failures.
evidence: tools/shared/exceptions.py:11-21 `class ToolExecutionError(RuntimeError)` with docstring "Raising one of these exceptions ensures the low-level server adapter marks the result as an error while preserving the structured payload we pass through the exception message"
Raise sites (source only): server.py:842, server.py:862, tools/clink.py:749, tools/challenge.py:156, tools/simple/base.py:304/403/570/580/588, tools/workflow/workflow_mixin.py:650/743/755/1569/1583

SDK: `.venv/.../lowlevel/server.py:472-479 _make_error_result(...) → CallToolResult(content=[TextContent(text=error_message)], isError=True)`; `585-586 except Exception as e: return self._make_error_result(str(e))`

Regression test exists: tests/test_mcp_error_handling.py:40-63 drives `mcp_server.request_handlers[CallToolRequest]` directly and asserts `server_result.root.isError is True` and that the text parses as JSON with `status == "error"`
why: The contract works but is stringly-typed: the structured payload survives only because `str(exception)` happens to be the JSON. Any future `raise ToolExecutionError(...)` that adds a prefix, or any SDK change to the message it formats, silently turns a machine-readable error into prose. An `outputSchema` + `CallToolResult` return would make this explicit.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: An unknown tool name is answered with a normal success result — `[TextContent(text=f"Unknown tool: {name}")]`, `isError` false — and a test locks the behaviour in.
evidence: server.py:876-878 `# Handle unknown tool requests gracefully` / `else: return [TextContent(type="text", text=f"Unknown tool: {name}")]`
tests/test_server.py:13-19 `result = await handle_call_tool("unknown_tool", {})` … `assert "Unknown tool: unknown_tool" in result[0].text` — asserts content, never isError

Reachable in practice: the SDK skips validation when the tool is not in its cache (`.venv/.../lowlevel/server.py:487-495` `_get_cached_tool_definition` → logs "Tool '%s' not listed, no validation will be performed" and returns None), so the call falls through to PAL's handler
why: A host asking for a tool that does not exist is told it succeeded. Agents that branch on isError will treat a typo'd or disabled tool (`DISABLED_TOOLS`) as a normal answer and feed the string "Unknown tool: x" into their reasoning. One-line fix (`raise ToolExecutionError`), but the existing test asserts the current shape and must change with it.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: Errors from non-tool handlers take a completely different path: `handle_get_prompt` raises `ValueError(f"Unknown prompt: {name}")`, and the SDK converts any handler exception outside call_tool into `ErrorData(code=0, message=str(err))` — a JSON-RPC error whose code is 0, which is not a code the MCP spec defines.
evidence: server.py:1397-1399 `logger.error(f"Unknown prompt requested: {name}"); raise ValueError(f"Unknown prompt: {name}")`
`.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/server/lowlevel/server.py:791-794` `except Exception as err: if raise_exceptions: raise err; response = types.ErrorData(code=0, message=str(err), data=None)`

server.py:1500-1502 calls `server.run(read_stream, write_stream, InitializationOptions(...))` with no `raise_exceptions` argument; SDK default is `raise_exceptions: bool = False` (`.venv/.../lowlevel/server.py:646-661`)
why: Two error dialects on one server: tools get isError+JSON, prompts get a JSON-RPC error with a meaningless code. This is inherited SDK behaviour, not PAL's choice, but it is PAL's surface — and it is the same class of opacity CHANGES-FORK.md:85 already complains about ("From the client side that surfaces only as a bare `-32000`").

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: PAL emits no progress notifications of any kind. There is no reference to `send_progress_notification`, `report_progress`, `progressToken` or a progress token anywhere in the source, despite the SDK exposing both the sender (`ServerSession.send_progress_notification`, session.py:462) and the token (the request's `_meta` reaches handlers through `RequestContext`).
evidence: `grep -rnE "report_progress|send_progress_notification|progressToken|progress_token" --include=*.py .` (.venv excluded) → no matches (exit 1)
The word "progress" in source appears only as in-band JSON status strings, e.g. tools/analyze.py:545 `f"{tool_name}_in_progress": "analysis_in_progress"`, tools/planner.py:324, tools/tracer.py:337

SDK plumbing is present: `.venv/.../lowlevel/server.py:758-763` constructs `RequestContext(message.request_id, message.request_meta, session, …)`; `.venv/.../lowlevel/server.py:605` reads `req.params.progressToken` for the inbound direction
why: The single most valuable unused primitive for this codebase, given PROG-02. Progress notifications are also how many hosts decide a call is alive rather than hung — emitting them is the standardized version of half of what epic #11/#15 is building a bespoke session registry to achieve.
search_boundary: All *.py outside .venv, four spellings (camelCase and snake_case, sender and receiver names). Also confirmed no MCP logging notifications: `send_log_message` has zero source hits in the same sweep.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: Long-running work is real and completely silent. `clink` allows a child CLI to run for 1800 s by default and reports nothing to the host until the subprocess exits; a 672 s call has been measured. The host, not PAL, is what keeps such calls alive.
evidence: clink/constants.py:8 `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 1800`; clink/constants.py:25 `timeout_seconds: int = DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`

clink/agents/base.py:284-298 `stdout_bytes, stderr_bytes = await asyncio.wait_for(process.communicate(prompt.encode("utf-8")), timeout=self.client.timeout_seconds)` — one collection at the end, nothing streamed

docs/reports/2026-08-04-clink-phase0-spike-host-followup-and-cli-capability.md (measured table): `codex / gpt-5.6-sol @ high` → `duration_seconds` **672.15**, success; four of five calls exceeded 120 s

Same report: at 120 s Claude Code emitted *"MCP tool \"pal/clink\" is still running after 120s. It was moved to the background as task `<id>` … you'll receive a notification with the result when it completes"* — host-side backgrounding, and the report labels the other three hosts (codex, cursor, antigravity) UNMEASURED, with codex's own transport observed dying mid-run (`worker quit with fatal: Transport channel closed, when Auth(AuthorizationRequired)`)
why: PAL's survival on long calls is currently a property of one host's fallback behaviour, measured on one day with five samples, and the report itself says so. A progress notification per child event would make liveness PAL's own guarantee across all four hosts instead of a lucky inheritance.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: The data a progress stream would carry already exists and is thrown away: clink's clients emit line-oriented JSON events (codex `--json`, opencode `--format json`, claude JSONL) which PAL's parsers consume — but only after `communicate()` returns the whole buffer at process exit.
evidence: clink/agents/base.py:284-288 single `process.communicate(...)` under `asyncio.wait_for` — no incremental read loop

Parsers are event-per-line by construction: CHANGES-FORK.md:~150 "OpenCode runs headless as `opencode run <message> --format json`, emitting one JSON event per line"; clink/parsers/claude.py:46/82 `_build_metadata(payload, stderr)`; conf/cli_clients/codex.json:4 `"--json"`
The parsed events already carry usable milestones — e.g. opencode's `type:"step_finish"` with `part.tokens` and `part.cost` (CHANGES-FORK.md, opencode section)
why: Turning progress on is not "invent a progress model": it is replacing one `communicate()` with a line-reading loop that already has a parser waiting for each line. Cost is one function in clink/agents/base.py; the payoff is per-step visibility on 30-minute calls plus the liveness signal of PROG-02.

area: MCP protocol surface — how PAL presents itself to a host (server entry point, capability d
statement: Every tool already returns a Pydantic-modelled JSON envelope (`ToolOutput`, with a 13-value `Literal` status) serialized to a text blob — and the pinned SDK will populate `structuredContent` automatically for any handler that returns a dict, validating it against `outputSchema` if one is declared. PAL declares no `outputSchema` and returns `list[TextContent]` everywhere.

statement: PAL guesses the host's transport budget rather than negotiating it: `MCP_PROMPT_SIZE_LIMIT` is computed from the `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` environment variable (60% of it, at 4 chars/token) and falls back to a hardcoded 60,000 characters. Over the limit, the tool returns an in-band `resend_prompt` status instructing the agent to write the prompt to `prompt.txt` and call again.

why: The protocol has no size-negotiation primitive, so a heuristic is defensible — but the heuristic is keyed to one host's environment variable (`MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is Claude's), and the fallback is a constant. Any other host gets 60,000 characters whether that is right or not. It also means one of PAL's 13 control statuses exists purely to work around an unmeasurable limit, which is another argument for making those statuses machine-readable (OUT-01).

statement: The server is genuinely async and dispatches tool calls CONCURRENTLY on a single event loop in a single process: the MCP SDK spawns each incoming request as its own anyio task, so N in-flight clink calls are N coroutines sharing one thread.
evidence: server.py:1500 `async with stdio_server() as (read_stream, write_stream):` then `await server.run(...)`; server.py:1519 `asyncio.run(main())`

No thread offload anywhere on the request path: `grep -rn "to_thread|run_in_executor" --include=*.py .` outside .venv returns only clink/agents/antigravity.py:128
why: Everything below follows from this: there is exactly one thread doing all the work, so any synchronous call anywhere in any tool stalls every concurrent clink subprocess drain at once. Anyone building the #20 supervisor must assume real concurrency already exists and is unregulated.

providers/gemini.py:205-206 `max_retries = 4` / `retry_delays = [1, 3, 5, 8]` → 17s of synchronous sleep worst case

area: Concurrency and performance model of the PAL MCP server fork (D:/Github/pal-mcp-server), w
statement: MEASURED: the clink timeout handler `process.kill()` then `await process.communicate()` with NO timeout, and when the CLI has spawned a grandchild that grandchild inherits the stdout pipe, so the second `communicate()` never returns. The `CLIAgentError("timed out after N seconds")` is therefore never raised — the caller is never told the run timed out, and the coroutine is pinned until the orphan exits.
evidence: clink/agents/base.py:284-292: `stdout_bytes, stderr_bytes = await asyncio.wait_for(process.communicate(prompt.encode("utf-8")), timeout=self.client.timeout_seconds)` / `except asyncio.TimeoutError as exc:` / `process.kill()` / `drained_stdout, drained_stderr = await process.communicate()` — the second call has no `wait_for`

stdlib asyncio/subprocess.py `_read_stream`: `output = await stream.read()` (read to EOF) then `await self.wait()`; asyncio/streams.py `read(n=-1)`: `while True: block = await self.read(self._limit); if not block: break; blocks.append(block)` — EOF only arrives when EVERY handle on the pipe's write end is closed

EXPERIMENT run on this machine (Windows 11, CPython 3.11, Proactor loop), reproducing base.py:284-292 exactly with a child that spawns a grandchild inheriting stdout/stderr: output was `first communicate timed out as expected` / `second communicate() STILL BLOCKED after 14.02s` / `direct child returncode: 1` — i.e. the direct child was terminated and the drain still never returned

Live on this machine for the `cursor` client: ~/.pal/cli_clients/cursor.json sets `"command": "C:/Users/xenod/AppData/Local/cursor-agent/cursor-agent.cmd"` — a .cmd batch file, which CreateProcess runs by launching cmd.exe, which launches the real agent: a guaranteed grandchild
why: Issue #20's problem statement says `process.kill()` "terminates the CLI process but not its descendants". The reality is worse and changes the fix: the run does not merely leak a process, it never reports at all. Any supervisor built on top must drain with its own deadline and close the parent's pipe handles, not just target the process group — process-group kill alone still leaves the second `communicate()` waiting if a descendant escaped the group.
search_boundary: The hang is verified with a synthetic grandchild, not with a real CLI (I did not spawn codex/claude/agy). The mechanism (pipe write-handle inheritance) is measured; that a given real CLI creates a pipe-inheriting grandchild is verified only for the .cmd shim shape.

area: Concurrency and performance model of the PAL MCP server fork (D:/Github/pal-mcp-server), w
statement: The antigravity runner's deadline sits immediately BEFORE a call that can block forever, so a silent `agy` is never timed out and its `to_thread` worker is held indefinitely. pywinpty defaults to blocking reads, which also makes two branches of that loop dead code.
evidence: clink/agents/antigravity.py:195-207: `while True:` / `if time.monotonic() - start > timeout: timed_out = True; break` / `try: data = proc.read()` / `except EOFError: break` / `elif not proc.isalive(): break` / `else: time.sleep(0.05)`
pywinpty 3.0.5 (.venv/Lib/site-packages/winpty/ptyprocess.py:32) `self.read_blocking = bool(int(os.environ.get('PYWINPTY_BLOCK', 1)))` — blocking by default
ptyprocess.py:181-196 `def read(self, size=1024):` docstring "Can block if there is nothing to read." and body `data = self.fileobj.recv(size)` — a blocking socket recv with no timeout

ptyprocess.py:343-355 `_read_in_thread`: `data = pty.read(blocking=blocking) or '0011Ignore'` then `client.send(...)` — with blocking=True nothing is sent while the PTY is silent, so the `'0011Ignore'` empty-data sentinel (which the agent's `elif`/`else` branches exist to handle) is never produced
why: docs/OPEN-WORK-LEDGER.md already lists 'PTY timeout may not interrupt a blocking read' as a hardening item without a mechanism. This is the mechanism, and it says the fix is not 'harden the teardown' but 'stop using a blocking read' — set PYWINPTY_BLOCK=0 or read on a deadline — because no teardown code is ever reached.

statement: A doc claim in the repo is now stale and should not be planned against: `_run_in_pty` DOES call `proc.close(force=True)`, which reaches pywinpty's `terminate(force=True)` and TerminateProcess-es the direct agy process. The 2026-07-16 report's 'the agy subprocess is never killed' is wrong for the direct child; it remains true for descendants, and it is unreachable anyway when the read blocks (C5).

statement: `add_turn` is a lock-free read-modify-write over shared storage: it reads the whole thread, appends, and writes it back. The storage lock covers each get and each set individually but not the pair, so two concurrent clink calls on one `continuation_id` silently lose a turn.
evidence: utils/conversation_memory.py:354 `context = get_thread(thread_id)` … :371-372 `context.turns.append(turn)` / `context.last_updated_at = ...` … :384 `storage.setex(key, CONVERSATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, context.model_dump_json())` — no lock spans these

utils/storage_backend.py:36 `self._lock = threading.Lock()`; :52-56 `def set_with_ttl(...): with self._lock:`; :58-70 `def get(...): with self._lock:` — per-operation only, no compare-and-swap, no transaction

Two independent writers exist per clink call: server.py:775 `arguments = await reconstruct_thread_context(arguments)` writes the USER turn, and tools/clink.py:367 `metadata.update(self._record_turn_and_total(continuation_id, content, request, model_info))` writes the ASSISTANT turn
why: This is the one piece of genuinely shared mutable state on the clink path and it is unprotected. It also corrupts the #26/#77 cost accounting: `_thread_totals` (tools/clink.py:511) sums the turns that survived, so a lost turn silently under-reports spend. Cheap fix (a lock or a compare-and-set in the storage backend) with no design work required.

statement: On a continuation call, clink synchronously reads and line-numbers EVERY file referenced anywhere in the thread, on the event loop, before the subprocess is spawned. Measured on this machine: 11 ms for a 64k-token file budget, 51 ms for a 320k-token budget, warm cache.
evidence: server.py:775 `arguments = await reconstruct_thread_context(arguments)` runs for any call carrying a continuation_id, BEFORE the `if name in TOOLS` dispatch, so clink is not exempt despite `requires_model()` being False

utils/conversation_memory.py:843 `formatted_content, content_tokens = read_file_content(file_path)` in a plain `for file_path in files_to_include:` loop

utils/file_utils.py:487-489 `with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f: file_content = f.read()` then :493 `file_content = _add_line_numbers(file_content)` (utils/file_utils.py:255, a full-string rebuild)
Budget: utils/model_context.py:135-145 — `content_ratio 0.8`, `file_ratio 0.4` → file_tokens = 32% of the context window; 64k tokens for a 200k-ctx model, 320k for a 1M-ctx model

statement: Antigravity concurrency is capped at 24 simultaneous calls by the default asyncio thread pool on this machine, and each call additionally costs a pywinpty reader thread and a loopback TCP listener — a per-call resource footprint the pipe runners do not have.

statement: Synthesis — what 10 concurrent clink calls actually do: 10 anyio tasks on one loop, 10 subprocesses spawned with no cap, all in PAL's cwd with PAL's full environment; ~110–510 ms of aggregate blocking file I/O if they are continuations; full transcripts accumulating in memory with no bound; and any one of them that times out never returns and pins its task forever.

area: How PAL actually runs — operations, observability, packaging (D:/Github/pal-mcp-server)
statement: The antigravity ConPTY timeout cannot fire while the child is silent. `_run_in_pty` checks the deadline only at the top of each loop iteration, but `proc.read()` performs a blocking `socket.recv` — pywinpty's reader thread only forwards its `'0011Ignore'` keepalive when a non-blocking `pty.read` returns falsy, and blocking mode is the default (`PYWINPTY_BLOCK` defaults to 1). A live-but-silent `agy` therefore blocks the worker thread indefinitely, past `timeout_seconds`.
evidence: clink/agents/antigravity.py:194-207 — loop: `if time.monotonic() - start > timeout: timed_out = True; break` then `data = proc.read()`
clink/agents/antigravity.py:128-130 — `await asyncio.to_thread(self._run_in_pty, ...)`; `asyncio.to_thread` cannot cancel a running thread
.venv/Lib/site-packages/winpty/ptyprocess.py:181-186 — `def read(self, size=1024): """... Can block if there is nothing to read."""`
.venv/Lib/site-packages/winpty/ptyprocess.py:193 — `data = self.fileobj.recv(size)` (blocking socket)
.venv/Lib/site-packages/winpty/ptyprocess.py:32 — `self.read_blocking = bool(int(os.environ.get('PYWINPTY_BLOCK', 1)))` — blocking by default

.venv/Lib/site-packages/winpty/ptyprocess.py:353 — `data = pty.read(blocking=blocking) or '0011Ignore'` — the keepalive is only produced when the blocking read returns, so it does not arrive during a silence
why: clink's 1800s child timeout is the operator's only backstop against a wedged delegation, and for antigravity it is unenforceable. In practice `agy`'s own `--print-timeout` (default 5m) usually saves it — but that is the child's discipline, not PAL's, and it does not cover a hung or non-responsive binary. A read deadline (socket timeout) or a watchdog that force-closes the PTY would make the declared timeout real.

area: How PAL actually runs — operations, observability, packaging (D:/Github/pal-mcp-server)
statement: `shlex.split()` (POSIX mode) silently destroys Windows absolute paths in a client config's `command` field — and that field is exactly what the fork's own documented override mechanism tells users to fill with an absolute path. Note the asymmetry: `additional_args` ARE handled correctly via expanduser/expandvars, so the same path works as an argument and breaks as a command.
evidence: clink/registry.py:189 — `tokens = shlex.split(command)` — default posix=True

Demonstrated with the repo's own interpreter: `.venv/Scripts/python.exe -c "import shlex; print(shlex.split(r'C:\Tools\agy.exe')); print(shlex.split(r'C:\Program Files\x\agy.exe'))"` → `['C:Toolsagy.exe']` and `['C:Program', 'Filesxagy.exe']`

The documented pattern that hits it — conf/cli_clients/claude-9arm.json.example: `"command": "REPLACE_WITH_ABSOLUTE_PATH_TO_claude.exe"`, with `_comment` instructing 'fill in your own claude.exe path'
CHANGES-FORK.md:195-207 documents `~/.pal/cli_clients/` overrides as the way to point at custom paths, persisting across reinstalls
The asymmetry: clink/registry.py:144 — `config_args = [os.path.expandvars(os.path.expanduser(a)) for a in raw.additional_args]` — args get correct treatment, command does not
Downstream, the mangled string has no separator left, so clink/discovery.py:52-53 (`if os.sep in command or (os.altsep and os.altsep in command)`) treats it as a bare name and PATH lookup fails
Workaround verified: `shlex.split('C:/Tools/agy.exe')` → `['C:/Tools/agy.exe']`, and `os.altsep == '/'` on Windows, so forward slashes survive both the split and the discovery check
Listed as still-open in docs/reports/2026-07-16-clink-brainstorm-gap-analysis.md §3.2
why: The fork's primary platform is Windows and its primary extension point is `command`. The user follows the .example file, gets `Executable 'C:Toolsagy.exe' not found in PATH` — a path they never typed — and has no way to connect that to shlex. Two viable fixes: accept a list-valued `command` (as pkg gap analysis suggests), or pass `posix=False` on Windows. Documenting the forward-slash workaround in the .example file is the zero-risk interim step.

statement: Every foreign CLI subprocess inherits PAL's entire environment via `os.environ.copy()`, including every provider API key (OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, DIAL_API_KEY, CUSTOM_API_KEY). There is no allowlist.

statement: Every CI workflow runs on `ubuntu-latest`. There is no Windows runner, so the fork's primary platform and all of its Windows-specific code — the ConPTY runner, pywinpty, discovery's `%LOCALAPPDATA%`/`%APPDATA%` lookups, and the shlex path handling — are never exercised. evidence: `grep -n "runs-on" .github/workflows/*.yml` → docker-pr.yml:22, docker-release.yml:20, semantic-pr.yml:19, semantic-release.yml:15, test.yml:9, test.yml:39 — all `ubuntu-latest`, no `os:` matrix key anywhere

statement: The file-access guard's Windows entries are hardcoded to the C: drive and omit the 32-bit program directory: `DANGEROUS_SYSTEM_PATHS` contains only `C:\Windows` and `C:\Program Files`, and `DANGEROUS_HOME_CONTAINERS` only `C:\Users`. statement: Operator-facing message quality is uneven and splits cleanly. GOOD: no-API-key at startup enumerates all six accepted variables; a missing CLI binary names the executable and the client; clink timeout names the client and the second count; agy's own print-mode deadline is specifically detected and explained rather than misattributed; antigravity's model-vs-effort conflict names both values. BAD: a stale cached CLI path reports 'not found in PATH' for a CLI that is on PATH (win-03/start-03); the Linux pywinpty message is actively wrong (win-06); a shlex-mangled path is echoed back in its mangled form; a non-zero agy exit that is not a timeout is blamed on the model ('a requested model may be unsupported/rejected') regardless of actual cause; and a failure to create the log directory prints only to stderr, which MCP clients usually discard.
evidence: Good — server.py:545-553 lists GEMINI_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY / XAI_API_KEY / DIAL_API_KEY / OPENROUTER_API_KEY / CUSTOM_API_URL

Good — clink/agents/antigravity.py:148-153 detects 'timeout waiting for response' and explains `--print-timeout` semantics; the reasoning is documented in tests/test_clink_antigravity_timeout.py ('A wrong cause costs more than a vague one, because it sends the reader somewhere')

Bad — clink/agents/antigravity.py:155 `detail = "a requested model may be unsupported/rejected"` for every non-timeout non-zero exit

why: The good cases show the codebase already has the discipline (the timeout fix even has a test whose docstring argues the principle). statement: calculate_token_allocation reserves 40% (context < 300,000) or 20% (>= 300,000) of the context window for the response without ever consulting capabilities.max_output_tokens, so gemini-2.5-pro reserves 209,715 tokens for a model that can emit at most 65,536 — 144,179 tokens (13.7% of the window) reserved for output that cannot exist.
